answers.answer: The 81 percent figure is agreement among humans themselves, so it is the target the judge is measured against rather than a perfect score. Before reporting either figure the authors define agreement: the probability that two randomly selected, non-identical individuals of each type agree on a randomly selected question. Without that definition a percentage is uninterpretable, since it says nothing about which pairs were drawn or what counted as agreeing. The 85 percent figure is also scoped to one setup, S2 without ties.
accept: identifies 81 percent as human-human agreement, so it is the realistic ceiling or comparison target rather than perfection
states that agreement was defined before any number was reported
describes the definition as a probability over pairs of randomly selected non-identical judges of each type on a randomly selected question

answers.answer: Any two of: position bias, fixed by presenting the pair in both orders and requiring the verdict to survive the swap, since only GPT-4 was consistent in more than 60 percent of cases; verbosity bias, favouring longer responses even when they are not clearer or more accurate; self-enhancement bias; and failure on math and reasoning questions the judge does not know the answers to, which means holding those out or supplying a reference. Two mitigations carry measured effects: a few-shot judge raised consistency from 65.0 to 77.5 percent, and reference-guided grading moved a failure rate from 70 to 15 percent.
accept: names two of position bias, verbosity bias, self-enhancement bias, and failure on questions the judge cannot answer
gives a concrete harness change, such as swapping presentation order and requiring the verdict to survive, or supplying a reference answer, or few-shot examples
attaches at least one measured figure to a bias or a mitigation

answers.answer: It does not carry over. ARES reports that judges fail to generalise across drastic domain shifts, naming switching languages, switching from text to code, and switching from retrieving text to extracting entities, webpages, or citations. Judge-Bench found reliability on some tasks with substantial variability by the property evaluated, the expertise of the human judges, and whether the language is human or model-generated, and recommends validating a judge against task-specific human annotations before deploying it for any particular task. So the judge needs revalidating on the new task with fresh human labels.
accept: says the existing validation does not transfer to the new domain
names at least one of the measured shifts, such as text to code or extraction of entities and citations
states the recommendation to validate against task-specific human annotations before deployment

answers.answer: A mixed paragraph is neither true nor false as a unit, so scoring it whole produces an average nobody can act on. Decomposing it into short focused assertions, which is the stated aim of the step, lets each assertion be checked against the retrieved context on its own, so the score becomes a count of grounded versus ungrounded claims and points at which claim failed. This is done without a gold answer, since the metrics are self-contained and reference-free.
accept: says a whole answer mixing grounded and invented claims cannot be judged true or false as a unit
says each short assertion is checked separately against the retrieved context
connects this to scoring without a gold or reference answer

answers.answer: Precisely one thing is changed between the current system and the proposed one, and a small proportion of traffic, given as 1 to 10 percent of users, is randomly directed to the variant while most users stay on the current system. One change at a time is what makes an observed difference attributable, and random assignment is what makes the two groups comparable. The source's stated reason for the method's popularity is that A/B tests are easy to deploy, easy to understand, and easy to explain to management.
accept: one thing changed between current and proposed system
a small proportion of traffic, around 1 to 10 percent of users, randomly directed to the variant while most stay on the current system
easy to deploy, understand, and explain to management

answers.answer: An A/B test splits users into two groups, each seeing one variant. Interleaving gives the same user both variants and infers the preference from that user's actions, so the comparison happens within a session rather than across two populations. Airbnb measured about a 50X speedup over A/B on their traffic. That result comes from search ranking on an accommodation marketplace, with listings and clicks as the actions, and nothing in the chapter measures interleaving for a retrieval-augmented assistant, where what action reveals a preference between two prose answers is unsettled. Interleaving there was used to select candidates for A/B testing, not to replace it.
accept: A/B splits users between variants, interleaving shows one user both and reads preference from their actions
cites roughly a 50X speedup over A/B measured on Airbnb traffic
names the domain limit: search ranking on a travel marketplace, not generated answers, so the number does not transfer
notes interleaving selects candidates for A/B testing rather than replacing it

answers.answer: The measurement establishes that the system's output changed on a fixed corpus and question set, scored by a stand-in judge. It establishes nothing about users, because no user was present. None of the sources in this chapter establishes what a reference-free score on a replayed dataset predicts about live outcomes: RAGAS and ARES both validate against human annotations rather than following a system into production. The nearest evidence is Airbnb's finding that purely offline evaluation was not accurate enough for candidate selection, because the ranker evaluated only sees what the logging ranker showed, and that is search ranking rather than an assistant. It says offline was insufficient, not how the two modes relate.
accept: the replay result is about behaviour on a fixed corpus and question set, scored by a proxy
the claim about users is not established, since no user was involved
states that no source in the chapter links a reference-free replay score to live outcomes, without claiming nobody has ever studied it
cites the Airbnb offline limitation, the logging ranker's visibility, as the nearest evidence and names its domain

answers.answer: Anything the dataset cannot contain. The answers were produced from a single introductory section of a Wikipedia page, so the set holds short answers about recent encyclopaedia events grounded in one paragraph. A failure on a long document with contradictory sections, or in another language, or on a question needing several sources reconciled, has no instance in the set to fail on, so the score cannot register it. The stand-in did not judge those cases unimportant; it never made them available, which has the same effect on the dashboard. Labels come from two annotators, and Judge-Bench found measured quality varies with the expertise of the human judges.
accept: names a failure the dataset has no instance of, such as long or contradictory documents, other languages, or multi-source questions
explains that the score is silent because the case never appears in the set, not because it was judged unimportant
identifies the dataset and its labels as a chosen stand-in for the truth

answers.answer: Live traffic shows what real people did after the change reached a random slice of them, which a replay cannot show at all because no person is in it. The mechanics ration that evidence: one thing changed, and only 1 to 10 percent of users randomly directed to the variant while the rest stay on the current system, so the arm you care about fills slowly. Airbnb is the worked case, since their users travel about twice a year and A/B testing alone is often insufficient there because of the long running times experiments require. What arrives is behaviour, not explanation: return visits are an indirect measure of satisfied users, and relevance stands in because user happiness is elusive to measure. The cost is real user exposure plus elapsed time.
accept: says live traffic shows what real users did after the change reached a random slice of them, which a replay cannot show because no user is involved
names the A/B mechanics that ration the evidence: one change, a small randomly assigned share of traffic to the variant, most users left on the current system
ties the waiting time to the product's own traffic rather than to the team's schedule, using the low usage frequency of this product or the Airbnb case as the example

states that the resulting signal is indirect or behavioural, so it does not establish why users acted, citing return visits as an indirect measure or relevance standing in because happiness is elusive to measure
identifies the cost as real user exposure plus elapsed time
